content:
Apple is required to respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with the Brazilian antitrust regulator. Epic accuses Apple of adopting a restrictive interpretation of its obligations under a recent antitrust settlement concerning the App Store in Brazil. The following are the details of the incident.

Background

Two months ago, Apple announced that it now allows developers to distribute apps through alternative app marketplaces in Brazil.

This change was part of a settlement that resolved a years-long antitrust investigation. The investigation stemmed from a complaint filed by Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple has also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% Core Technology Fee on sales of digital goods and services made inside apps distributed through channels outside the App Store. Click here for more details on the structure.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to Brazil's O Globo (via MacMagazine) today, Epic recently filed a petition with CADE, the Brazilian antitrust regulator, accusing Apple of creating "structural, technical and access barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic says that, although the new Brazilian terms apply only to iOS apps, the agreement Apple reached with CADE "explicitly covers iPadOS."

The company is also reported to have objected to so-called "scare screens," arguing that these screens discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store. Epic also criticised the current installation process, saying it requires nine steps, three more than the solution Apple currently implements in Europe.

O Globo reports that Epic added that Apple's initial installation process in Europe required 15 steps, but after being forced to reduce this to six steps, "the download abandonment rate fell from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "go far beyond what is needed to calculate fees," allowing it to "monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo reports that CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
